paper_title: DeltaStreamer: Towards Human-Like Agentic Streaming Video Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change-aware memory with query-driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively. Project page: https://bbbbchan.github.io/DeltaStreamer/

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Streaming video is prevalent in real-world applications such as live surveillance [13], robotics [4, 44], and autonomous systems [54, 43], where visual input arrives continuously rather than as complete clip. Unlike offline video, where the entire sequence is available for analysis, streaming video arrives frame by frame. The system can access only what has already been observed and must operate continuously without seeing future frames [18]. Questions may also arrive after the relevant events [82]. The system must therefore build and maintain memory without knowing which details will later be needed. Existing offline video models [78, 46] struggle to adapt to the streaming setting, which requires continuous perception, incremental memory updates, and on-demand responses. Recent work has begun to address these challenges using token compression [5], KV-cache reuse [21, 8], and multi-turn dialogue [59, 51]. Despite the progress, these directions share two limitations in streaming scenes. First, their records primarily capture what is present while leaving what is changing implicit. Consecutive frames often contain similar scene content [80], so repeated representations can consume the available budget and obscure the transitions that distinguish events. Second, once frame has passed, the evidence is limited to what is retained from the visual signals [70]. Without mechanism to revisit the original frame, details omitted during observation cannot be recovered when later question makes them relevant. Both limitations reflect that existing paradigms focus on managing the token budget, with insufficient attention to recording changes and recovering missing evidence. This motivates us to investigate more natural and intuitive way for streaming video understanding. We argue that the system should watch frame by frame, just as human does, continuously observing, building and updating structured memory. As frames arrive sequentially [53, 15] and queries arrive independently, the system needs to process visual information and update memory asynchronously [30, 29]. Before query arrives, it should retain broad visual evidence without knowing which details will later matter. When question arrives, 1 Fig. 1 Comparison of streaming video understanding paradigms. Compression or truncation in KV-cache reuse and multi-turn dialogue can obscure transitions and discard details needed by later queries. DeltaStreamer records explicit changes in structured memory and uses query-driven planning and targeted replay to recover missing visual evidence. it should actively probe its memory, assess whether the retrieved evidence is sufficient, and revisit historical frames to recover missing pixel-level details for well-grounded answer. We should view streaming video understanding as an active information-gathering [83, 57] problem rather than passive encoding task, calling for an agent that extends VLM with planning and tool use [52]. Recent efforts such as StreamAgent [61] and EventMemAgent [58] have explored this agentic direction, but they share the same limitation that stored representations may omit evidence needed for later queries. In this paper, we build DeltaStreamer, human-like agentic streaming video understanding system that continuously builds hierarchical textual memory from incoming frames and actively gathers evidence in response to user queries, just as human viewers follow video as it unfolds, remember what happened, and revisit earlier footage when memory falls short. Considering that consecutive frames may yield similar scene descriptions even when important changes occur, the system compares adjacent frames during observation and explicitly records their visual changes as deltas alongside scene descriptions. These observations are organized into hierarchical textual memory, with source links connecting summaries to their supporting observations and video frames. When query arrives, query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and whether it should be sought in past, current, or incoming frames. The resulting plan remains available throughout subsequent reasoning, guiding memory retrieval, continued observation, and tool use. When retrieved descriptions lack required visual detail, the agent can follow the source links to locate relevant historical frames and replay them to recover pixel-level evidence. Unlike previous works that mostly focus on compressing and retaining video history, we couple explicit change recording with persistent query-driven planning and targeted replay. This allows the agent system to reason over event transitions and recover query-relevant visual details omitted from memory. We evaluate DeltaStreamer on OVO-Bench [33] and StreamingBench [28], where it outperforms representative methods from existing streaming video understanding paradigms. In summary, our contributions are: We propose DeltaStreamer, an agentic streaming video understanding system inspired by human observation and active investigation. It continuously builds structured memory and, after query arrival, uses planning and tool use to gather evidence until it can answer. We design delta-augmented hierarchical textual memory that explicitly records inter-frame changes alongside scene descriptions. three-layer DAG with bidirectional cross-layer pointers and an entity index makes these records traceable across temporal scales. We introduce query-driven planner that performs structured analysis of the querys needs and produces persistent plan to guide memory retrieval, continued observation, and tool use. Targeted replay recovers pixel-level visual details missing from textual memory.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Streaming Video Representations and Memory. Streaming video understanding requires continuous processing and selective retention of historical evidence. Existing approaches support these requirements through token compression [25, 45, 55, 19], KV memory [47, 2, 42, 77], and multi-turn dialogue [65, 60, 6]. TimeChatOnline [67] removes redundant tokens using inter-frame differences, ReKV [11] retrieves historical KV states, and StreamMem [64] maintains compressed, query-agnostic KV memory. Streamo [59] develops instruction tuning for streaming interaction. Other approaches explicitly organize history for later queries. StreamForest [68] constructs an event-level memory forest, WAT [17] separates query-independent watching from query-triggered thinking, and Vista [31] recalls full-resolution historical evidence from compressed scene representations. Together, these methods establish mechanisms for retaining and accessing video history. Some works also begin to enhance understanding quality from an omni-modal perspective [7, 56, 79, 62]. DeltaStreamer focuses on making semantic changes explicit and traceable. It directly compares adjacent sampled frames and stores the resulting deltas alongside scene descriptions in hierarchical memory with source links and an entity index, connecting recorded transitions to supporting visual evidence. Agentic Evidence Gathering. Streaming agents [81, 22, 69] extend memory retrieval with planning and tool use. StreamAgent [61] explores anticipatory planning for online interaction. EventMemAgent [58] combines event memory, visual anchors, and inter-event change logs with learned memory search and visual tool use. OASIS [26] uses an adaptive coarse-to-fine process that generates retrieval intents and retrieves event memory with keyframes. Different from them, DeltaStreamer couples direct inter-frame change recording with structured plan specifying the query target, temporal anchors, and required evidence. The plan remains available to guide subsequent retrieval and tool rounds, including targeted historical-frame replay when stored observations lack decisive details.

sections.title: 3.5 Look-Back Verification and Replay
sections.content: To ground answers in visual evidence beyond stored descriptions, we combine memory consistency checks with targeted replay of historical frames. Replay has two entry points. The agent can request missing visual details, or verifier can flag unresolved conflicts among retrieved records. Both routes inspect retained historical frames through replay(τ ), where τ is target frame index available from the current index t, with 0 τ t. Before candidate answer is accepted, rule-based verifier checks records retrieved using the planners retrieval query. The verifier groups claims by subject and property and applies lightweight cross-layer consistency and temporal heuristics. Unresolved conflicts with available historical frames become replay candidates. For verifier-triggered candidates, heuristic priorities favor severe conflicts and frames closer to the question time. The scheduler selects = arg max ρ(u), τ = τu , uUt: ρ(u)>η (5) Here, is the current frame index and Ut contains unresolved conflicts with available replay targets. For conflict u, ρ(u) is its heuristic priority, η the threshold, and τu its frame index. The highest-priority eligible conflict yields replay frame τ = τu . With no eligible candidate, the verifier requests no replay. After inspecting the historical frame, the agent resumes investigation at the current frame, using additional visual evidence to generate an answer or re-evaluate. Appendix A.5 details the conflict rules, priorities, and candidate limit.

sections.content: 4.2.1 Compared Methods We compare proprietary models, open-source offline models, and streaming systems. Proprietary models include Gemini 1.5 Pro [48], Gemini 3 Flash1, and GPT-4o [34]. Offline models include Qwen2-VL-7B/72B [50], Qwen3VL-8B [3], LLaVA-Video-7B [76], LLaVA-OneVision-7B (LLaVA-OV) [24], InternVL2-8B [9], InternVL38B [84], LongVU-7B [40], LongVA-7B [75], VILA-1.5-8B [27], VideoLLaMA2-7B [10], and Gemma3-4B [49]. Streaming systems include HERMES [73], VideoLLM-online [6], OASIS [26], SimpleBaseline [41], FOLIO [12], Stream-IT [51], JoyAI-VL-Interaction [66], LatentStream [36], Mage-VL [63], Flash-VStream [71, 72], Dispider [35], ReKV [11], StreamForest [68], Streamo [59], VST [16], ViSpeak [14], TimeChat-Online [67], QueryStream [74], LiveVLM [32], STRIDE [20], StreamAgent [61], and EventMemAgent [58]. Human results are provided by the respective benchmarks. 4.2.2 Benchmark Results OVO-Bench. Tab. 1 reports an overall score of 66.07 for DeltaStreamer, gain of +5.32 points over EventMemAgent. It also outperforms Gemini 3 Flash by +2.05 points, with higher scores on action-sequence identification, hallucination detection, and repeated-event counting. The method reaches 79.05 on action-sequence identification (ASI) and 69.89 on hallucination detection (HLD). Its improvements on these tasks align with our emphasis on distinguishing events and gathering evidence relevant to question. StreamingBench. Tab. 2 reports an overall score of 59.53, exceeding STRIDE by +1.95 points and also outperforming StreamAgent. Contextual understanding improves over STRIDE, with scores of 55.20 on MCU and 47.60 on SQA. Summaries preserve temporal coverage but cannot retain every detail later question may require. Selective recall restores relevant older observations that are absent from the summaries and outside the recent window. The model can therefore use compact temporal overview together with detailed source evidence selected for the question. Removing replay lowers accuracy to 63.28, the largest drop among tool removals. Pre-query observation cannot anticipate every future information need. Middle recall recovers details already stored as text, while replay can supply visual evidence that was never encoded, explaining its value alongside structured memory. Zoom and tracking also help by exposing fine spatial details and supporting correspondence of the same target across frames. These capabilities address complementary evidence needs; each ablation removes one capability with the remaining tools available.

sections.title: 4.4 Qualitative Analysis
sections.content: Fig. 4 illustrates the complementary roles of change-aware memory and query-driven evidence gathering. Explicit changes help represent event progression when successive frames contain similar scene content, while observations provide temporal anchors for later reasoning. However, textual memory can retain scene without preserving every detail that future question may require. The planner connects the querys information needs to relevant observations and guides historical visual inspection when stored descriptions are insufficient. This enables the agent to reason over retained evidence and recover omitted visual details on demand.

sections.title: 5 Conclusions
sections.content: In this work, we introduce DeltaStreamer, human-like agentic framework for streaming video understanding. It records explicit inter-frame changes in traceable hierarchical memory to preserve event transitions for later queries. query-driven planner specifies evidence needs and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay when evidence is insufficient. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench, together with ablations, demonstrate the benefits of combining change-aware memory with planned evidence gathering. These findings support streaming paradigm in which systems continuously observe and remember, then actively investigate when question arrives.

sections.title: A Methodology Details
sections.content: A.1 Observation Scoring Details For the novelty score in Eq. 2, the history window contains up to 12 recent observations. Field tokens are extracted using regular-expression matching, converted to lowercase, and deduplicated. The field weights are 0.35 for delta, 0.25 for actions, 0.15 for actors, 0.10 for objects, 0.10 for OCR, and 0.05 for scene; description receives the default weight of 0.05. Delta receives the largest individual weight to prioritize explicit visual changes when assessing new information. With no observation history, nonempty observation receives novelty 1. field without matching historical token set has maximum similarity 0, and an observation with no nonempty token set receives novelty 0. Salience converts novelty into weight for later retrieval, increasing the priority of observations that add information beyond recurring scene descriptions. For novelty 0.3, salience is 1 + 0.5s and the observation is marked as change-bearing; otherwise, salience is 0.5. separate repeated-delta guard demotes repeated templates to salience 0.5 and clears the change flag. This decision uses the full structured observation and repetition checks, including when the delta reports verified-static frame. The associated change flag also determines whether group of observations satisfies the change requirement for episodic aggregation. A.2 Memory Construction and Rendering Stored records and cross-layer links. Working events retain their timestamp, observation text, delta, salience, change flag, referenced frame, and optional parent episode identifier. Episodes store their time span, summary, and supporting working-event identifiers. Long-term pins retain their source episode identifier and are created from model-emitted recap blocks or automatically promoted episode boundaries. Separate reverse pointers support navigation in both directions without introducing cycles into the hierarchys directed abstraction edges. An episode need not have long-term pin to support workingepisodic retrieval. A.2.1 Episode Construction Episodes can be created as new observations arrive or when memory is prepared for model call. Online boundary detection identifies when to close the current episode, while aggregation and coverage rules summarize observations that have not yet been assigned to one. The model can also request an explicit episode through Recap. Online boundaries. run is the sequence of working observations accumulated since the previous online boundary. Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (BOCPD) [1] estimates whether an incoming observation continues this sequence or begins new one. boundary is proposed when the most probable hypothesis has index zero, indicating new sequence, and the accumulated run contains at least three observations. Before accepting it, content-continuity check compares the incoming observation with the first observation of the run. If their scene descriptions match and their estimated actor counts agree, with both fields available, the boundary is suppressed to avoid splitting continuous scene. Otherwise, the accumulated observations are summarized and linked to an episode, the detector is reset, and the incoming observation starts the next run. Aggregation and coverage. Some working events are not assigned to an episode by online boundary detection. When rendering memory, the system groups these uncovered events chronologically, starting new group when consecutive events are more than 10 seconds apart or including the next event would extend the group beyond 45 seconds. Groups with at least five events and one change-bearing observation are retained. Adjacent retained groups are then merged when their mean field-level Jaccard similarity is at least 0.85 and their temporal gap is at most 30 seconds. This consolidates observations that describe similar content; the 45-second limit applies before merging. The change requirement can leave long, mostly static intervals without an episodic summary, even though their observations remain in working memory. coverage fallback therefore checks the interval after the latest episode and before the recent observations still shown individually in visible memory. If this interval spans at least 30 seconds, uncovered events are split into initial groups of at most 45 seconds, with at least two events per group, and the same similarity-based merging is applied. These groups become anchor episodes with lower 17 base salience, preserving temporal coverage without requiring detected change. well-formed model-emitted Recap also creates an explicit episode and corresponding long-term pin. A.2.2 Entity Index and Memory Rendering The entity index records each entitys working-event identifiers, first and most recent timestamps, and observed surface names. Entities are extracted from observation text by rule-based matching. Cross-frame references are linked conservatively through name normalization, including matching generic head noun to more specific compound name, such as man and man in white. compact digest exposes frequently mentioned entities and their temporal spans. Evidence paths. Among query-matching records, Backtrack in Eq. 3 selects at most two long-term pins, three episodes, and three working events as starting nodes, excluding question pins and planner notes. Source expansion includes at most three working events per episode. Paths receive ranking bonus for covering multiple memory layers, are deduplicated by their starting node, and are returned in descending score order up to the requested limit. The layer quotas allow at most eight paths. Visible memory. Recall in Eq. 3 ranks keyword-matching working records using salience, change bonus, and recency, with an additional token-hash similarity score when cached embeddings are available. The renderer takes the highest-ranked candidates and retains those in the middle interval, excluding entries already covered by the visible head or recent tail. The selected observations are displayed chronologically. Because this filtering follows retrieval, the recalled set can contain fewer records than the requested limit. Query construction removes answer-option text, common instruction words, and duplicate tokens from the question and the need field. Rule-based matching interprets the free-form temporal scope, evidence type, and strategy to derive an evidence category and tool-use guidance. Appendix E.3 provides the planning instruction and the runtime template for persistent plan fields and the evidence contract. A.4 Evidence-Gathering Tools We expose each tool through shared description template specifying its name, purpose, and JSON argument schema. To request execution, the agent emits <tool_call> block with name and arguments fields, then waits for the result before continuing. The shared call template and instructions for interpreting results and selecting subsequent tools are reproduced in Appendix E.4. The tools in Tab. 7 use SAM2 [39] for object tracking and Whisper [38] for speech transcription. Post-query model calls receive single current frame, with additional images supplied by spatial tools. Tool rounds can continue at the same frame, whereas continued observation advances to new frames. Interpretations of tool results also update memory. Tools return <tool_result> block containing their name, success status, and result or error. successful zoom additionally supplies the crop as an image input to the following model call. Replay returns the selected replay time and schedules historical-frame inspection through the temporal controller. When the seek is applied, the historical frame becomes the visual input, and the previous stream position is retained for return. Tab. 7 Tool suite of DeltaStreamer, grouped by function. Recover visual details omitted from textual memory. Crop and zoom into sub-region of the current frame with IoU-based deduplication to prevent redundant zooming. Efficiency set_sample_rate Adjust the observation frame rate (0.252.0 fps) during static periods to save computation. 19 A.5 Look-Back Verification and Replay Details Replaying historical frames incurs substantial overhead through additional frame access and visual processing, which can delay responses. We therefore use the checks and priority rules below to assess whether unresolved conflicts justify this cost before triggering automatic replay. Claim extraction and initial checks. When invoked, the verifier requests up to 16 evidence paths, subject to the layer quotas described in Appendix A.2. Claim extraction uses fixed text patterns for explicit state tags, location phrases, limited set of attributes, and numerical counts. Subject and property strings are lowercased, and claims about the same subject and property are grouped. The following preliminary rules are applied in order. The first matching rule skips subsequent cross-layer and temporal checks for that group and triggers no automatic replay. These outcomes concern the need for replay and do not establish that the proposed answer is visually correct. 1. group with fewer than two claims is marked uncertain and does not trigger replay. 2. If working and episodic records contain the same set of values but long-term records differ, the group passes the initial check. 3. If every gap between consecutive claims in temporal order is at most 2 seconds on the stored 1-fps timeline, the group passes the temporal-proximity check. 4. If all claims have the same value, the group passes the agreement check. 5. If at least 85% of claims share one value, the group is marked uncertain without replay. Conflict severity and target selection. Groups unresolved by the preliminary checks are examined for disagreement across memory layers and state transitions that may need visual confirmation. The cross-layer check gives greater weight to records closer to the original observations. The temporal check can flag transitions that may reflect missing intermediate evidence, even when the cross-layer check requests no replay. Either check can nominate replay candidate, whose severity reflects the stronger signal. For cross-layer conflict, the verifier targets the earliest supporting working observation when available. flagged temporal transition supplies its earlier endpoint if no target is selected. The scheduler then ranks these candidates to decide whether and where to look back. Replay priority. For conflict with severity cu and replay index τu, the implemented priority in Eq. 5 is ρ(u) = [prep max(0, 1 cu)] max(dmin, 1 λ time(τu) time(tq)) , (8) Here, is an unresolved conflict, ρ(u) is its replay priority, cu is its conflict-severity score, and τu is its target sampled-frame index. tq is the question-arrival frame index; time maps frame indices to video timestamps in seconds, and the absolute-value term is their temporal separation. prep is the schedulers assumed correctness after replay; max(0, 1 cu) is its heuristic estimate without replay. dmin is the minimum temporal weighting factor and λ is its decay rate per second. Defaults are prep = 0.95, dmin = 0.5, and λ = 0.02 s1. Candidates with ρ(u) η are discarded, where η = 0.15 is the minimum priority required to justify replay cost; the remainder are sorted by descending priority, deduplicated by target, and capped at three.

sections.title: B Benchmark Details
sections.content: Evaluation protocol. Query times beyond the supplied video segment are mapped to the last available frame. Planning and finalization calls can reuse the last available frame without exposing additional video. Accepted responses and their trigger times are read from the recorded outputs, and task-specific parsers extract the required answer format. Question and response times refer to video timestamps rather than wall-clock inference time. B.1 OVO-Bench OVO-Bench [33] contains 3035 evaluation samples spanning 12 tasks in three groups. The Real-Time Visual Perception group (837 samples) includes Optical Character Recognition (OCR), Action Recognition (ACR), Attribute Recognition (ATR), Spatial Understanding (STU), Future Prediction (FPD), and Object Recognition (OJR). The Backward Tracing group (631 samples) includes Episodic Memory (EPM), Action Sequence Identification (ASI), and Hallucination Detection (HLD). The Forward Active Responding group (1567 samples) 20 includes Repetition Event Count (REC), Sequential Steps Recognition (SSR), and Clues Reveal Responding (CRR). B.2 StreamingBench StreamingBench [28] contains 4500 QA samples in three groups. The Real-Time Visual Understanding group covers Object Perception (OP), Causal Reasoning (CR), Clips Summarization (CS), Attribute Perception (ATP), Event Understanding (EU), Text-Rich Understanding (TR), Prospective Reasoning (PR), Spatial Understanding (SU), Action Perception (ACP), and Counting (CT). The Omni-Source Understanding group covers Emotion Recognition (ER), Scene Understanding (SCU), Source Discrimination (SD), and Multimodal Alignment (MA). The Contextual Understanding group covers Anomaly Context Understanding (ACU), Misleading Context Understanding (MCU), Sequential Question Answering (SQA), and Proactive Output (PO).

sections.title: D Discussions
sections.content: D.1 Limitations DeltaStreamer requires repeated model and tool calls, which may increase inference latency, although frame arrival and processing can proceed asynchronously in real-world streaming settings. Compact visible memory also leaves storage costs for records and historical frames. Errors in observations or temporal anchors can affect retrieval, while agreement across memory layers does not ensure perfect correctness. Our evaluation uses one shared backbone on two benchmarks and leaves challenges in historical event localization, sequential-step recognition, and proactive response timing. The weaker PO results on StreamingBench highlight the additional challenge of precise response triggering, since retrospective evidence recovery cannot compensate for missed response window. Further work should examine other backbones and the trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and storage. D.2 Broader Impacts DeltaStreamer may support accessibility tools and help users review extended activities by retrieving relevant historical evidence. However, continuous observation, structured memory, and replay can expose personal routines and facilitate non-consensual monitoring. Errors or biases may propagate through stored descriptions and answers, misrepresenting peoples actions. For deployment, we recommend informed consent from recorded individuals, limited retention, access controls, and deletion mechanisms covering both frames and derived memories. Human review of the underlying evidence should precede consequential decisions about individuals. These applications and the effectiveness of the recommended safeguards have not been evaluated in this work.

sections.title: E Prompt Templates
sections.content: E.1 Pre-Query Observation The two-line instruction applies to the ordinary observation report followed by </Silence>. Tool calls occupy intermediate turns, after which the agent is prompted again on the same frame. conditional <Recap> block may precede </Silence>, as described in Appendix E.2. The prompt requires concrete change while forbidding invented changes, with exceptions for the initial frame and verified identical frames.

sections.title: Observation prompt
sections.content: [Phase] OBSERVE-ONLY. The question has not been asked yet. Reply with EXACTLY two lines: Line 1: <Observation> SELF-CONTAINED FULL frame report covering ALL SEVEN labelled fields below, in this order, on EVERY frame (no exceptions, no abbreviations, no same as before, no bare (no change)): description: 1-2 sentences, holistic summary of THIS frame. BAD: "A kitchen scene." GOOD: "Medium shot of chef in white uniform standing at stainless-steel counter, chopping carrots with chefs knife. Steam rising from pot on the stove in the background." actors: EVERY distinct person/animal visible. For each: appearance, clothing, role, position. Re-list ALL actors every frame. Include background figures. Always state the TOTAL count (e.g. 2 actors: ...). BAD: "actors: person cooking" GOOD: "actors: 1) chef in white double-breasted jacket, black apron, toque, at center counter chopping; 2) sous-chef in blue polo, at back sink washing dishes" objects: salient objects with current STATE and LOCATION. Tag state explicitly. For COUNTABLE objects, report the EXACT number (e.g. 3 cards, 5 bottles) never vague ranges like approximately 3-5 or several. Format: <object> [state] at <location> BAD: "objects: knife, pot, carrots" GOOD: "objects: chefs knife [held, in use] in chefs right hand; large stockpot [on stove, steaming] back left; 3 carrots [being chopped] on cutting board center frame" actions: what each actor is CURRENTLY doing (verb + target + state tag). Format: <actor> <verb> <target> [STATE] State tags: [STARTING] / [IN-PROGRESS] / [FINISHED] / [ABORTED] BAD: "actions: cooking" GOOD: "actions: chef chopping carrots [IN-PROGRESS]; sous-chef washing dishes [IN-PROGRESS]" For persisting actions, use still ... or continues to ... instead of re-describing. ocr: EVERY on-screen text/number VERBATIM. Include language, color, position. BAD: "ocr: some text on screen" GOOD: "ocr: CHANNEL 5 NEWS (white text, top-left overlay); scoreboard reads HOME 24 - 18 AWAY (yellow, bottom-right); subtitle: What are you doing? (white, bottom-center)" If genuinely no text: "ocr: (none)" 23 Observation prompt (continued) scene: location + time-of-day + camera framing + indoor/outdoor. BAD: "scene: indoors" GOOD: "scene: professional kitchen, daytime (fluorescent lighting), medium-wide shot, eye-level angle, indoor" delta: what CHANGED from the PREVIOUS frame. This is the MOST IMPORTANT field it drives memory compression and retrieval. MUST name at least one concrete, observable change. Format: <subject> <verb/delta> <detail> BAD: "delta: slight motion" (generic boilerplate) BAD: "delta: no change" (NEVER allowed) BAD: "delta: scene continues" (garbage token) GOOD: "delta: chefs right hand moved 3cm left, knife blade angle changed from 30 degrees to 45 degrees" GOOD: "delta: steam plume above stockpot expanded upward approximately 5cm; new bubble formation visible" GOOD: "delta: sous-chef turned head 90 degrees left toward chef; mouth opened (speaking)" If you GENUINELY cannot detect any change after active visual inspection, pick tool (zoom_crop / track_query) to find evidence first. ONLY if the frame is bit-identical may you write: "delta: visually identical to t={prev}s verified static".</Observation> CRITICAL when at least two entities of the same kind are visible: COUNT them exactly (e.g. 5 giants, 3 dogs, 2 cars) and describe their relative spatial order (front/back/left/right/foreground/background, or in row from left to right: A, B, style). Identify which one is biggest / closest / leftmost this is exactly the kind of fact future question may rely on. Line 2: </Silence> (status tag meaning "observed, no answer yet"). Do NOT emit </Response>. The system reads <Observation> into MEMORY and uses </Silence> as the round-end marker. Anti-Hallucination Rule Every delta: field MUST reference SPECIFIC VISIBLE elements that YOU CAN SEE in the CURRENT frame(s). Do NOT speculate about off-screen events or future actions. Do NOT infer intentions unless there is explicit visual evidence (e.g., facial expression, pointing gesture). If uncertain about detail (count, color, identity), write [uncertain: <detail>] rather than guessing. For ANY claim involving COUNT or COLOR, visually re-examine the frame before writing do not trust memory. The delta MUST describe change you SEE between the two frames; do not invent changes to satisfy the format. Initial-frame instruction [Round 0 initial frame, no previous frame to compare] Write full observation; set delta to (initial frame). Fig. 6 Observation-prompt excerpts, including the seven report fields and visual-grounding rules, followed by the separate initial-frame instruction. The literal {prev} is retained from the static-frame example. E.2 Memory Summarization and Online Recaps The following templates are separate text-only summarization calls; their scheduling and memory links are described in Appendix A.2. Here, {t0} and {t1} are interval endpoints, {len(run)} is the number of input observations, and {body} is their text.

sections.title: Auxiliary memory summarization prompts
sections.content: Episodic summary System message. You compress run of streaming-video observations into ONE concise episodic summary. Output 1-3 sentences (at most 120 words total) covering: actors involved, the ordered action chain, final scene state, and any salient changes. Do NOT include per-second timestamps in the body. No markdown, no lists, no preamble just the summary text. User message. Window [t={t0}s, t={t1}s], {len(run)} events: {body} Write the summary now. Long-term record System message. You distil run of streaming-video observations into durable LONG-TERM FACT record. Prioritise FACT COVERAGE over brevity: capture EVERY concrete fact present all actors (with exact counts), all key objects (with counts), the action(s) performed and their final state (started/in-progress/finished), locations and spatial relations, and any visible on-screen text/numbers. Prefer listing more facts to omitting them. Do NOT speculate beyond the observations and do NOT invent details. Output plain prose or semicolon-separated facts (no markdown, no preamble, up to approximately 6 sentences). User message. Segment [t={t0}s, t={t1}s], {len(run)} observations: {body} Write the fact-covering long-term record now. Fig. 7 Complete system and user templates for the two auxiliary memory-summarization calls. The Recap instruction applies at semantic boundaries within frame-processing turns before or after query arrival. It does not require separate summarization call.

sections.title: Online Recap instruction
sections.content: Recap on semantic boundaries (REQUIRED when applicable) If THIS frame marks semantic boundary an event you were narrating just FINISHED, SCENE CHANGE happened, an ACTOR ENTERED / LEFT / visibly CHANGED, or KEY OBJECT appeared/disappeared/changed state additionally emit <Recap t0=<sec> t1=<sec> kind=<event_end scene_changeactor_enteractor_exitactor_changeobject_changemilestone> state=<finishedstarted in_progressaborted>> ... </Recap> block in this same turn (BEFORE </Silence>). The state= attribute is REQUIRED on event_end / milestone / object_change / actor_change recaps. It tells future readers (and event-state/answerability meta-questions) the EXACT progression status of the event: state=finished: the action / step is FULLY COMPLETED (use this when narrating event_end). Future Online Recap instruction (continued) event-state queries can use this as completed evidence. state=started: the action has just begun, evidence is now observable but not yet completed. Future answerability queries can use this as onset evidence. state=in_progress: the action is mid-stream; completion not yet reached. state=aborted: the actor visibly stopped or abandoned the action without finishing. The Recap body MUST start with an explicit verb phrase that names the state, e.g. "FINISHED: <action> at t=12s", "STARTED: <action> at t=8s, currently in progress". This single phrase is what future memory_search will surface for state queries. The Recap should be 38 sentences and MUST cover: every actor involved (with appearance), the full ordered action chain in [t0,t1], final state of key objects (use one of: present/absent, open/closed, on/off, full/empty, moving/static), spatial layout at the boundary, any on-screen text / dialogue verbatim, and why this is boundary. The system pins it as durable long-term memory. Do NOT emit Recap on quiet frames; do NOT emit more than one every approximately 5 seconds. E.3 Query-Driven Planning The complete planning-phase instruction is followed by its acknowledgement and the template inserted into subsequent answering calls.

sections.title: Planning prompt
sections.content: [Phase] QUESTION POSED PLANNING STEP (analyse BEFORE you answer). The question is below (and pinned to MEMORY). Do NOT answer yet and do NOT call tools this turn. First THINK about what the question truly asks, then emit ONE <Plan> block: <Plan> need: <in your own words, the exact thing being asked the TARGET and its ANCHOR (the moment/event/actor it pivots on)> pov: <FIRST-PERSON CHECK does the question say "I"/"me"/"my"? If so, "I" am the CAMERA WEARER, NOT any person fully visible in the frame. The camera wearers own hands/arms/legs appear entering from the BOTTOM or EDGE of the frame; person sitting across the table fully facing the camera is the OTHER person, NOT me. State clearly WHO "I" am and WHO the other people are here. Note my own body is often only partially visible or off-screen, so question about what do may not be answerable by looking at me directly> info_type: <what KIND of evidence settles it e.g. temporal order of actions / spatial direction or position / existence (is even present?) / exact count / object identity / attribute like color> Planning prompt (continued) evidence_locus: <work out WHERE the deciding evidence for THIS question lives in your own words, no default direction. Weigh three possibilities even-handedly and pick whichever the question truly calls for: (i) it is in the CURRENT frame / the moment the question is asked (what is happening or visible right now); (ii) it is in something that has ALREADY happened (recorded in MEMORY / specific past moment to re-look); (iii) it has NOT happened yet and you must keep observing until it does. Do not assume it is in the past just because MEMORY is handy, nor in the present just because frame is in front of you. Check the ANCHOR the question pivots on (e.g. the event in "what happens AFTER X" / "before X"): has that anchor and the thing asked relative to it actually appeared yet? If not, the evidence is not in hand and answering now would just guess from whatever is nearest. Then say how youll obtain it: look at the current frame, read/search MEMORY layer (for what terms), replay specific moment (which and why), or keep watching. If the target is hard to observe directly (occluded, off-screen, or your own body), infer it INDIRECTLY from observable traces how the objects it acts on changed, the before/after scene difference, or the effect it left> answerability: <look at the ACTUAL listed OPTIONS (A/B/C/D...) as CLOSED set your final answer MUST be one of them verbatim. Check whether one of THOSE listed options literally says "Unable to answer" / "cannot determine" (or similar). Do NOT count the generic instruction to "give best-guess if uncertain" as such an option that is NOT choice, and there is no "implied" unable option. If such choice IS listed: your first job is to VERIFY the target exists before locating it, and you may pick it when the evidence truly shows the target is absent. If NO such choice is listed: refusing is FORBIDDEN even with weak evidence you must commit the single MOST LIKELY listed option, never "Unable to answer". State here which case this is> meta: <is the question asking whether something CAN be answered / WILL happen / has STARTED-vs-FINISHED (a meta/state question), rather than plain fact? yes/no + why> strategy: <turn your evidence_locus reasoning into concrete plan: given WHERE you decided the evidence lives, spell out which memory layer to read/search (and for what terms), whether the current frame suffices, and which exact to replay if you need to confirm. E.g. for an action-order question: locate the exact of the anchor action, then read the NEXT action change after it. For direction question: compare two frames few seconds apart, do NOT track. For an existence question: search once or twice; if empty AND "Unable to answer" is LISTED option, answer it otherwise commit the most likely listed option. IMPORTANT if info_type is CURRENT-FRAME percept (what the person is doing RIGHT NOW, an on-screen object/text/attribute, an immediate action): the answer is in the CURRENT frame LOOK Planning prompt (continued) at it and answer directly. Do NOT replay the current moment (it just re-shows the same frame), do NOT browse other frames, and use at most ONE zoom_crop if detail is unclear. Commit quickly over-using tools on see-it-now question adds noise and flips close options (e.g. connecting vs disconnecting).> </Plan> End this turn with </Silence> right after the </Plan> block (you will be asked again immediately to act on this plan). The acknowledgement confirms that the plan was parsed. The stored plan is supplied separately in later calls.

sections.title: Tool use and question arrival
sections.content: Tool-call protocol Whenever you want to call tool, emit exactly the following block as part of your response (you may emit multiple such blocks): <tool_call>{"name": "<tool_name>", "arguments": {...}}</tool_call> After the tool block(s), STOP. The system will run the tools and feed <tool_result>{...}</tool_result> back to you. Only after you have enough evidence, finish with </Response> <your final answer>. Question-arrival instruction [Phase] QUESTION POSED. The question below is being asked NOW (and has been pinned to MEMORY). Read-the-question protocol (BEFORE deciding) Silently parse the question text into: TARGET: what is being asked (an entity, an action, count, Yes/No truth value, an on-screen text string, ...). ANCHOR: the time / event / actor it pivots on (e.g. right after loading the wheel, the person we communicated with while chopping, under the monkey at this moment). FORMAT: option letter, Yes/No, integer 0..N, free-form span match the wording exactly. Then check MEMORY for events that match the ANCHOR; the TARGET is whatever is reported in those events. If MEMORY only contains the ANCHOR but not the TARGET, the answer probably lies few frames later emit </Silence> and wait, OR replay to likely frame. Decide whether you can answer with the evidence accumulated so far (see MEMORY) or need to watch more frames (emit </Silence> to wait). GROUND YOUR ANSWER IN PIXELS WHEN IT HELPS: if the answer hinges on SPECIFIC PAST moment (an earlier action / object state / who was present), replay(t=...) that moment and verify with your own eyes before committing. YOU decide whether replay is needed and how many: questions about the CURRENT frame usually need none; questions about the past may need one or few. Do not over-replay when the current frame already answers it. BEFORE answering, prefer quick tool call if it would resolve uncertainty: To re-examine an earlier moment, use replay. To re-read your notes, use memory_read or memory_list. To inspect fine detail, use zoom_crop. If there is genuinely no visual evidence at all, abstain. One or two well-chosen tool calls almost always beat blind guess.

sections.title: Continued observation and evidence gathering
sections.content: [Phase] POST-QUESTION. The question is pinned in MEMORY (look for the [Q] ... entry). Continue watching the new frame. 29 Continued observation and evidence gathering (continued) Read-the-question protocol (every round) RE-READ the pinned [Q] ... line and parse it into TARGET / ANCHOR / FORMAT (see QUESTION POSED phase). Then ask: does the latest frame OR any new MEMORY event satisfy the ANCHOR? If yes, the TARGET is the fact reported there. First-Person POV: when the camera shows bare feet/legs/torso at the bottom of the frame, the camera wearer is I. question asking who did communicate TO or who did interact WITH is asking about the OTHER person NOT the one visible through the first-person perspective (that is I). Trace both peoples timelines in MEMORY: the camera-wearer (I) appears as partial body at frame bottom; the interaction partner is fully-visible actor. If the answer depends on SPECIFIC PAST frame, replay(t=...) that moment to CONFIRM with your eyes first; if the CURRENT frame or MEMORY already answers it clearly, just emit </Response> <answer>. Otherwise emit </Silence>. Use replay WHEN past moment needs verifying, but YOU decide if it is needed and how many; dont replay when the current frame already settles the answer. If something in MEMORY is fuzzy or this frame hints at the answer, use tool BEFORE answering replay to revisit past moment, zoom_crop for detail, memory_read to recall pinned fact, asr_segment for audio, or abstain if there is genuinely no evidence at all. CRITICAL: After EVERY tool result, FIRST write 1-2 line observation of what the tool revealed (especially: counts, text, identities, state changes) BEFORE you decide to call another tool. Do NOT chain tools blindly each tool call must be justified by specific gap in what you have ALREADY observed. If the tool result confirms what you need, COMMIT with </Response> NOW instead of calling more tools. zoom_crop that returns clear image of the target region IS ENOUGH write your observation and answer. If THIS frame marks semantic boundary (event ended / scene change / actor enter-exit-change / key object change), ALSO emit <Recap t0=<sec> t1=<sec> kind=<...>> ... </Recap> block (38 sentences, see OBSERVE-ONLY phase instructions for Recap format) the system pins it as durable memory. How to use the [RETRIEVED] block The [RETRIEVED ...] block above is the systems best-guess evidence for your question. HOW TO USE IT: Each path#N shows chain through memory layers (from wk to ep to lt). Follow the chain the working-layer event is closest to the original pixels. Cross-check: if fact appears consistently across working + episodic, it is reliable. If only in long_term, verify via replay. It is NOT exhaustive use memory_search with different keywords if needed. Tool selection (use BEFORE each call) 1. For MOVING subject across frames, use track_init (NOT zoom_crop). 2. If the answer depends on PAST frame, use memory_search first; if detail is missing, use replay. 3. If the cue is likely AUDIO, use asr_segment. 4. For STATIC fine detail in the CURRENT frame (text, label, logo), use zoom_crop. 5. To remember durable fact, use memory_write(pin=true). Anti-pattern: after 2 or more zoom_crops with no new fact, switch tools.
